items.title: Just bury your trash
items.author: Alex Chalmers and Rob Wiblin
items.blurb: Chalmers and Wiblin make the case that burying most waste in modern landfills beats recycling it — reusable substitutes like the cotton tote can take 173 times the energy of the disposable they replace.

items.title: AI hits college graduates in the heart of America’s data centre boom
items.blurb: Job postings in Texas have dropped for AI-exposed occupations, new research shows, squeezing college graduates in the middle of America’s data-centre building boom.

items.title: Bland new world: is AI making us all think the same?
items.author: Matthew Hutson
items.blurb: Researchers worry that generative AI is homogenizing culture and cognition, Hutson reports — one computer scientist says he keeps getting déjà vu reading recent papers in his field.

items.title: China’s real robot revolution is not about humanoids
items.blurb: China is applying its superpower of scaling and supply-chain building to industrial robotics, the FT argues — the challenge to the global industry lies there, not in humanoids.

items.title: How data centres became one of America’s hottest political issues
items.blurb: Growing hatred of the facilities is reshaping the midterm elections, the Economist reports — the AI data-centre buildout has become one of America’s hottest political issues.

items.title: Designing physics experiments with artificial intelligence
items.author: Jonathan Klimesch
items.blurb: A Nature Review surveys AI methods that now propose entirely new experimental layouts — configurations that often challenge established design conventions while matching or exceeding human-designed set-ups.

items.title: The College Wage Premium in the Generative AI Era
items.author: Tyler Cowen
items.blurb: Cowen flags a new paper: after four decades of expansion, the US college wage premium has fallen sharply since 2022 — implying an unprecedented drop in relative demand for college labour.

items.title: All the microbes you can’t have
items.author: Niko McCarty
items.blurb: McCarty traces how a decision to regulate engineered microbes under a 1976 industrial-chemicals law became a regulatory black hole: of more than 240 applications filed between 1987 and 2018, only a few were ever approved for widespread use.

items.title: Why you won’t get a flying car
items.author: Noah Smith
items.blurb: Smith reviews J. Storrs Hall’s progress-studies touchstone and finds in it the perfect encapsulation of what he calls ‘engineerism’ — the idea that if a technology can be built, we ought to build it — with both its value and its limits on display.

items.title: In an Age of AI, a Physicist Seeks What Endures
items.author: Rebecca Boyle
items.blurb: Sarah Demers, Yale’s physics chair, is leading the American Physical Society’s AI policy statement while never having typed anything into Claude or ChatGPT; she calls AI a godsend for tuning the Mu2e experiment but says it is forcing physicists to ask what is enduring about physics itself.

items.title: How Will the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act Affect Housing Supply? Part III
items.author: Brian Potter
items.blurb: Potter’s final instalment walks the remaining nine titles of the 59-section housing bill and finds the major supply impacts concentrated in a handful of sections — chiefly 501, 502 and 1001.

items.title: How Much Redistribution Will AI Require?
items.author: Alex Tabarrok
items.blurb: Tabarrok runs the numbers: if AI lifts growth to 10 percent a year, labour’s share can fall to 28 percent without cutting aggregate labour income, and even the techno-optimist scenario needs a transfer of only about 5.3 percent of GDP.

items.title: Nations expanding their research programmes impose sweeping penalties for malpractice
items.author: Benjamin Plackett
items.blurb: India, Peru and Vietnam are rolling out penalties for research misconduct — docked bonuses, restricted grant access, lower institutional rankings — as one audit found fabricated citations 12 times more common in 2025 than in 2023, Nature reports.

items.title: The moral panic over data centres is foolish
items.blurb: The Economist’s leader calls the growing backlash against data centres a moral panic fuelled by misinformation and misunderstanding.

items.title: Chinese businesses of all stripes are turning to Huawei
items.blurb: In industries from mining to transport, Huawei’s technology is becoming pervasive across Chinese business, the Economist reports.

items.title: Why I Want More AI at Dartmouth
items.author: Sian Leah Beilock
items.blurb: Dartmouth’s president makes the case for more AI in the classroom: universities that hide from the technology will merely secure their irrelevance, she writes.

items.title: America is still beating China in the AI race
items.author: Noah Smith
items.blurb: Smith argues the US is staying ahead of China in the AI race, though the costs of maintaining that lead are still unknown.

items.title: Anthropic AI ‘formalizes’ proof of Fermat’s last theorem in just 11 days
items.author: Davide Castelvecchi
items.blurb: Claude produced a 13-million-line, computer-checked proof of Fermat’s last theorem in 11 days, and mathematicians now expect AI to scrutinize, and perhaps overturn, results across the whole library of mathematics.

items.title: Has the A.I. Job Apocalypse Been Postponed?
items.author: John Cassidy
items.blurb: The spread of models like Claude and ChatGPT has not yet produced mass displacement of workers, but deployment is accelerating and economic pressures are rising.

items.title: AI keeps stubbornly refusing to take our jobs
items.author: Noah Smith
items.blurb: A Labor Day look at why, despite rapid AI adoption, human labor is still valuable and the predicted job losses keep failing to show up in the data.

items.title: Isaac Newton’s remarkable year — and the plagiarism accusations that followed
items.author: Andrew Robinson

items.title: Emergent Ventures winners, 59th cohort
items.author: Tyler Cowen

items.title: Social Media in China Is Getting Really Dark
items.author: Li Yuan

items.title: Does the U.S. need more spaceports?
How the Government Wastes Our Time
items.author: Adam Harris

items.title: Big US university endowments outperform S&P 500 index
AI Has Solved One of Math’s $1 Million Millennium Prize Problems
items.author: Konstantin Kakaes
items.blurb: OpenAI agents proved the Navier-Stokes equations can blow up in three dimensions, with the proof verified in Lean — but Kakaes reports a competing NYU group, and both teams built on techniques from mathematicians Córdoba and Martínez-Zoroa.

items.title: OpenAI claims huge maths breakthrough on a famed ‘Millennium Problem’
items.author: Davide Castelvecchi
items.blurb: Castelvecchi reports OpenAI’s claim to have cracked the physics of fluids using AI, solving one of the toughest puzzles in mathematics and a famed Millennium Problem.

items.title: The World Bank is right to prioritize reproducibility
items.blurb: A Nature editorial applauds the World Bank for publishing and verifying the raw data and code behind its research-based reports and papers, and says other agencies should follow.

items.title: No Doing, No Learning
items.author: Alex Tabarrok
items.blurb: Tabarrok argues that when regulation prevents an industry — nuclear power, engineered microbes — from ever existing, the loss is invisible: no one learns what they never got to do.

items.title: Sideline vested interests to reform China’s research
items.author: Qilin Zhang

items.title: OpenAI faces competing claims around maths breakthrough
Some Navier-Stokes updates
items.author: Tyler Cowen

items.title: Stop turning schoolchildren into crash-test dummies
God Help Us, Let’s Try To Learn About Mechanistic Interpretability Techniques
items.author: Scott Alexander

items.title: A data leak shut a top research biobank: lessons from the recovery
items.author: Diana Kwon

items.title: Limit bets on clinical-trial outcomes being placed on prediction markets
items.author: Thomas J. Hwang

items.title: Bosses are using AI to spy on employees' productivity—does it work?
Virtual worlds
Will Taiwan Just Give Up?

The 24-Year-Old Who Lost Billions
